description: 75% hydration sourdough gives an open crumb and a slack dough that needs stretch and folds. Work out the water, starter, and salt for any flour weight.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 325 g water, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. Total dough 885 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Total water is 75% of the flour: 500 × 0.75 = 375 g. Water to add is 375 - 50 = 325 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.

faqs.answer: Bread flour with around 12% protein or more. The extra protein builds the gluten network that holds a wet dough together. All-purpose flour at 10 to 11% protein can work at 75%, but the dough will be slacker and harder to shape, so hold back some water on your first try.
faqs.question: What flour works best at 75% hydration?

faqs.answer: Because the starter already brings water. For 500 g of flour, 75% hydration means 375 g of water in total, and 100 g of starter brings 50 g of that water. You add the remaining 325 g. Adding all 375 g on top of the starter would push the true hydration to about 77%.
faqs.question: Why is the water to add only 325 g and not 375 g?

felicityNote: Seventy-five percent is my weekend loaf, the one I bake when I have time to fold properly. The crumb is worth the wet hands.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 75%, every 100 g of flour holds 75 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add, holding back about 25 g of the water for now. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left. The dough will be soft and sticky. Add the held-back water only if the dough feels like it can take it.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then fold every 30 minutes for the first two hours: stretch and folds early, coil folds later when the dough is full of air.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, domed, and jiggly. Shape gently with a bench scraper and a light dusting of flour, then basket it seam side up.

howToSteps.name: Cold proof, then bake
howToSteps.text: Cover the basket and refrigerate overnight. Bake straight from the fridge in a hot Dutch oven: the cold dough scores cleanly and springs well.

lede: At 75% hydration the dough is slack and open-crumbed, the country-loaf territory where sourdough earns its holes. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter, so the hydration you ask for is the hydration you get.

name: 75% Hydration
summary: 500 g flour at 75% hydration: add 450 g flour, 325 g water, 100 g starter, 10 g salt.
title: Sourdough Calculator: 75% Hydration
tutorial: Seventy-five percent is where sourdough gets serious about crumb. The dough is slack, the holes open up, and the loaf eats the way a country sourdough should: a crackling crust, a custardy interior, and a crumb that tears in ragged pieces. It is also where handling starts to matter, because a 75% dough will not forgive a careless shape the way a 65% dough will.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 500 g of total flour at 75% hydration, the dough holds 375 g of water in total. Your starter brings 50 g of that water, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 325 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g.

Flour choice matters more at 75% than at lower hydrations. Bread flour with around 12% protein or more builds the gluten network that holds a wet dough together. The Perfect Loaf's country-style formulas sit around 75% with medium-protein bread flour, and they work because the flour can take the water. All-purpose flour at 10 to 11% protein absorbs less, so if that is what you have, hold back 25 g of water and add it only if the dough wants it.

Folding is the skill that makes 75% work. Stretch and folds early in bulk fermentation build strength, and coil folds later lift the dough without tearing the air out of it. Four to six sets in the first two hours will turn a dough that spreads like a puddle into one that holds its shape. Watch the dough, not the clock: it should feel tighter and smoother after each set.

Shaping a 75% dough is gentler than shaping a firm one. Use a bench scraper, a light dusting of flour, and quick, confident moves. A cold overnight proof in the fridge is your friend here: cold dough holds its shape, scores cleanly, and springs hard in a hot oven. Shape it, basket it, refrigerate it, and bake it straight from cold.
